title: Career Roadmap · Network Technician
summary: A Network Technician installs, configures, tests, maintains and troubleshoots computer networks. The role involves connecting computers and other devices, supporting routers and switches, resolving connectivity issues, maintaining network cables and assisting with network security.

about.label: Primary sectors
about.text: IT services, networking, telecommunications, cybersecurity, enterprise IT

about.label: Work environment
about.text: Offices, data centres, network operation centres, client sites and IT service environments

blocks.text: A Network Technician installs, configures, tests, maintains and troubleshoots computer networks. The role involves connecting computers and other devices, supporting routers and switches, resolving connectivity issues, maintaining network cables and assisting with network security.
Network Technicians help ensure that users and systems can communicate reliably across local area networks (LANs), wireless networks (WLANs) and, where relevant, wide area networks (WANs).

This career is suitable for students who enjoy troubleshooting, computer hardware, networking concepts and hands-on technical work. It also provides a foundation for progressing into network administration, network engineering, cloud networking or cybersecurity.

rows.text: Assist with cable testing, device setup, basic troubleshooting and ticket handling
Configure basic network devices, resolve connectivity issues and maintain network documentation
Handle more complex faults, monitor performance and support network changes
Design, optimise and manage larger network environments, subject to skills and qualifications

blocks.text: Career progression depends on hands-on experience, networking knowledge, certifications and the complexity of the systems managed.
The following plan assumes a three-year B.Voc programme. Adapt it to the actual syllabus and duration of the institution.
Year 1
Foundation
Build computer and networking fundamentals

items.text: Learn computer hardware, operating systems and peripheral devices.
Understand the OSI and TCP/IP models.
Study IPv4 addressing, subnet masks, gateways and DNS.
Learn Ethernet, MAC addresses, switches, routers and access points.
Practise Windows and Linux command-line networking tools.
Understand network cables, connectors, patch panels and basic cable testing.
Build small LANs using a network simulator.

blocks.text: Year 2
Technical skills
Develop configuration and troubleshooting skills

items.text: Practise subnetting and basic IPv4/IPv6 configuration.
Configure VLANs, trunk links and inter-VLAN routing in a lab.
Learn DHCP, DNS, NAT and routing fundamentals.
Understand Wi-Fi standards, encryption and wireless troubleshooting.
Study network monitoring, logs, packet captures and connectivity testing.
Learn firewall fundamentals, access-control lists and secure device configuration.
Practise documenting network diagrams, device inventories and support tickets.

blocks.text: Year 3
Job readiness
Prepare for professional network support

items.text: Build a simulated small-business network with separate user and guest networks.
Troubleshoot DNS, DHCP, addressing, routing and wireless connectivity faults.
Learn basic network monitoring and incident escalation.
Practise Wireshark packet analysis in an authorised lab.
Understand backup and recovery of device configurations.
Complete an internship with an IT support provider, network integrator or telecom company.
Prepare a portfolio containing network diagrams, configurations, troubleshooting reports and lab evidence.

blocks.label: Project 1
blocks.text: Small-office network simulation

Build a simulated office network with computers, switches, a router and separate departments. Configure IP addresses and demonstrate connectivity using Cisco Packet Tracer or another suitable simulator.

blocks.label: Project 2
blocks.text: VLAN and subnetting lab
Create separate networks for administration, employees and guests. Document the addressing plan, VLAN assignments and permitted communication paths.

blocks.label: Project 3
blocks.text: Network troubleshooting handbook
Document simulated faults such as incorrect IP settings, DNS resolution failures, disconnected cables and misconfigured gateways. For each case, record diagnostic steps and the verified solution.

blocks.label: Project 4
blocks.text: Basic network security lab
In an isolated lab, configure guest-network separation, secure administrative access and basic firewall rules. Explain how each control reduces risk.

blocks.label: Project 5
blocks.text: Network monitoring dashboard
Use sample or lab-generated data to report device availability, response times, downtime and common faults. Build the report in Excel or a suitable monitoring tool.

blocks.text: Certifications can help demonstrate knowledge, but they should complement practical lab experience.

blocks.text: After gaining experience, a Network Technician can move towards:

blocks.label: Network administration
blocks.text: Managing enterprise LAN and WLAN environments.

blocks.label: Network engineering
blocks.text: Designing and optimising routed and switched networks.

blocks.label: Wireless networking
blocks.text: Planning and troubleshooting Wi-Fi deployments.

blocks.label: Network security
blocks.text: Supporting firewalls, access controls and network segmentation.

blocks.label: Data-centre networking
blocks.text: Supporting physical connectivity and network equipment.

blocks.label: Cloud networking
blocks.text: Learning virtual networks, subnets, routing and cloud security controls.

blocks.label: Telecommunications
blocks.text: Working with ISP infrastructure, fibre and access networks.

By the end of the B.Voc programme, the student should aim to have:

items.text: Strong understanding of TCP/IP, IPv4/IPv6 and subnetting.
Hands-on lab experience with switches, routers, VLANs and basic routing.
Ability to diagnose common DNS, DHCP, cabling and wireless issues.
Familiarity with Windows and Linux networking commands.
Basic knowledge of network security and secure device configuration.
A small portfolio of documented networking projects.
An internship or practical exposure to IT support or network operations.
An entry-level certification, if suitable and affordable.

blocks.text: Final recommendation

For a Network Technician role, prioritise IP addressing, switching, routing fundamentals, systematic troubleshooting and practical lab work. Start with a network simulator, document every lab and practise explaining how you isolated each fault. Once these fundamentals are strong, an entry-level networking certification and an internship can help you compete for IT support, network support and NOC roles.
